title: Azure's First Dollar Figure Arrives With a Cash Problem Attached
subtitle: A $678 billion backlog looks bulletproof until you check how much cash it actually generates today.
summary: Microsoft will show exact dollar sales for Azure for the first time when it reports quarterly results on Oct. 28. The disclosure lands just as heavy capital spending squeezes cash generation across the artificial intelligence sector.

bodyHtml:
The market spent two years cheering every dollar poured into data centers. That party ended abruptly this month. Meta burned cash for the first time in a decade, credit default swaps widened across big tech, and chip stocks tumbled. Suddenly, capital expenditure on artificial intelligence is being judged as a financing bill rather than automatic growth.

Strip away the corporate jargon and Microsoft really sells two things. It sells software by the seat, bundling Outlook, Teams, and Copilot like a premium subscription you cannot cancel. And it rents out computing muscle by the hour through Azure. Azure is the electric utility of the generative boom: Microsoft buys the land, lines up the power, and installs the chips so everyone else can run their models.

On Oct. 28, investors will finally see Azure's quarterly revenue printed in exact dollars rather than vague percentages. A segment overhaul already recast the number. Azure brought in $29.42 billion during the June quarter, growing 42% under the narrower new definition against 43% on the old one, and topped $101.9 billion across fiscal 2026.

The headline case rests on the commercial backlog, which reached $678 billion in contracted work, up 84% in a year. A backlog is an unsigned tab at a bar. It promises future business, but it does not settle your power bill today.

The Numbers That Matter

The backdrop explains the nerves. Semiconductors are down more than 15% this month and memory names more than 20%, while software and cybersecurity are set to finish October higher. Meta's five-year credit default swap widened to a record, Nvidia's sits at 126 basis points, Oracle's at 343, and CoreWeave's has pushed past 11%. Evercore's Mark Mahaney expects the hyperscalers reporting this week to disclose as much as $100 billion more in capital spending.

Look beneath that backlog number and the concentration becomes clear. At the December quarter, Microsoft put about 45% of its then-$625 billion backlog on OpenAI, a single unprofitable customer that no longer has to use Azure exclusively. Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal on OpenAI's compute in the same October 2025 deal that added an incremental $250 billion Azure commitment.

Strip OpenAI out of the calculation, and the backlog grew 25% year over year. Microsoft holds about a quarter of OpenAI and booked a $5.0 billion non-cash gain on that stake in its last fiscal year. The startup currently flatters headline earnings rather than draining them.

To justify a higher valuation from here, Microsoft has to prove that ordinary corporate software buyers are driving cloud demand. The stock trades near 22 times forward earnings, which sounds reasonable until you notice what the multiple assumes. It assumes capital spending converts smoothly into high-margin enterprise sales. If IT departments balk at paying extra for automated office tools, that multiple has nowhere to go but down.

The bear case is that the backlog compounds faster than the cash it produces, and that accounting is left to cover the spread. Free cash flow fell 6.5% to $67.0 billion in fiscal 2026, a second straight annual decline, while capital spending swallowed about 44% of revenue. Build that quickly and depreciation follows. That expense jumped 84% in two years to $38.5 billion, now 11.6% of revenue.

Microsoft is also stretching the accounting life of its datacenters from 15 years to 25. Management says the change affects only the timing of future depreciation. The servers and GPUs that make up roughly two-thirds of the spend keep their short lives. If fiscal 2027 free cash flow sinks again, or if non-OpenAI backlog growth slides below 20%, the bears have it.

Bulls still have firepower. Azure growth held near 40% for three quarters, then hit 43% in the June quarter, and management guides 44% to 45% for the next one. Paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats crossed 30 million, with net seat adds more than doubling sequentially. Microsoft has also begun pushing its own Maia inference chips to cut reliance on merchant silicon. Cloud gross margin held near 66%, and management still guides to positive free cash flow for the year.

What we are watching in that report is whether Azure clears the 44% to 45% bar while capital spending crosses the guided $50 billion mark for a single quarter. The market is no longer buying artificial intelligence on layaway. Microsoft has to show that its largest commitments turn into cash before the depreciation bill does.
